title: Catherine of Siena
hook: a dyer's daughter who told popes what to do and nursed the plague-sick
carry: be who god meant you to be

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was behovely, and Julian's great promise to end the week: all shall be well. Your line was a love bigger than the hurt.

A letter opens warmly, calling its reader father. A few lines later it tells him, plainly, that he is failing and needs to be braver. The reader is the pope. The writer is a young woman from Siena, in Italy, with no title, no money and no official role. Nobody appointed her to advise the pope. She did it anyway. And between letters, she was nursing the plague-sick and burying the dead. Today: Catherine Benincasa.
screen: `A WARM OPENING.` → `BE BRAVER.` → `WRITTEN TO THE POPE.`

segments.voice: Catherine was the daughter of a wool dyer in Siena, one of the youngest of a very large family; tradition says more than twenty children. As a girl she decided to give her whole life to God. Her family pushed back hard, wanting her married. She refused. She didn't join a convent; she joined a group of lay women connected to the Dominican order, and lived at home, in a little room, praying. Then, in her twenties, she went out. She cared for the sick and the poor of Siena, and when plague came back, she nursed the dying and buried the dead. People gathered around her, friars, nobles, ordinary people, calling her mamma. And she spoke up. The popes then lived not in Rome but in Avignon, in France. Catherine was convinced the pope belonged in Rome. She told him so in letter after letter, and even traveled to Avignon to say it in person. The pope did return to Rome; historians still debate how much she influenced that. Tradition says she learned to write only late; she dictated most of her letters to friends. A famous saying of hers is on posters and mugs: be who God meant you to be and you will set the world on fire. Those exact words aren't hers. They're a loose modern version of a letter telling a friend that if he were what he ought to be, he'd set all Italy on fire. But the idea is truly hers. She died at thirty-three. In 1970 the Catholic Church named her a Doctor of the Church. Her boldness came from prayer, and it went out as love.
screen: `A DYER'S DAUGHTER.` · `THE PLAGUE-SICK OF SIENA.` · `LETTERS TO THE POPE.` · `SET ALL ITALY ON FIRE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've kept quiet about that might need saying, to a friend, a boss, a family member, a group: not a rant, one honest sentence said with love. Picture saying it the way Catherine began her letters, warmly, and then clearly, and notice any fear, and any care underneath it. If you pray, you can ask for courage and kindness together.
Catherine Benincasa. The dyer's daughter from Siena who nursed the dying and told popes the truth, with love.
Your line: be who God meant you to be. Warm first, then clear. Day two hundred seventy-four, in the books.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Catherine as a saint and Doctor of the Church, with a feast day on April 29, and Christians of other churches read her letters and her book, The Dialogue, as models of prayer that turns into bold action.
